title: Calder v. Jones (1984)
summary: California could hear the libel claim against the Florida author and editor because their allegedly intentional publication targeted California.
notes:
Walden requires a defendant-created forum connection; knowledge that a plaintiff resides in the forum, by itself, does not recreate Calder’s facts. This note supplies no full trial record.

The decision was unanimous (Rehnquist, J.); the defendants were National Enquirer reporter John South and president-editor Iain Calder, the Enquirer sold over 600,000 copies a week in California out of about 5,000,000 nationally, and the Court held that First Amendment concerns play no role in the jurisdictional analysis and that the defendants were not mere employees whose contacts are judged by the employer's.

sections.Parties: Jones, a California entertainer, sued the individual author and editor of an allegedly defamatory article, as well as interests associated with its publication.
sections.Material Facts: The article concerned the California activities of a California resident and relied on sources connected to that state. California was a substantial audience for the publication, and the alleged reputational injury was expected to be suffered there. The individual defendants worked in Florida, but the content and dissemination of their alleged wrong focused on California.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court upheld the exercise of personal jurisdiction over the individual defendants. The assigned book presents the case in a short note accompanying the modern specific-jurisdiction cases.
sections.Issue: Could intentional out-of-state publication create a sufficient relationship between its author and editor and the forum where the alleged wrong was focused?
sections.Holding: Yes, on these facts. California was the focal point of the alleged conduct and harm.
sections.Reasoning: The defendants’ location when writing and editing did not exhaust the geographic meaning of their conduct. Their alleged acts concerned a person’s California activities, drew on California information, and were directed toward a publication with a major California audience. That combination connected the defendants themselves to the state. The analysis also did not recognize a special First Amendment exemption from otherwise valid personal jurisdiction.

learning.why: California could hear the libel claim against the Florida author and editor because their allegedly intentional publication targeted California.

topics.cp-effects-test: The alleged intentional libel focused on California through its subject, sources, circulation, and expected harm.
topics.purposeful-availment: The individuals’ own alleged conduct connected them to the forum.
topics.cp-personal-jurisdiction: The author and editor required their own jurisdictional analysis even though the employer circulated the publication.
topics.minimum-contacts: The case treats intentional targeting as supplying the contacts that make individuals answerable in the forum.
topics.relatedness: The libel claim arose directly from the California-focused article.

mnemonic.rationale: A National Enquirer story about an actress
